 Medicare Advantage selection system is a disaster | Letter 
 Consumers need and deserve clarity.

 The Medicare Advantage system is broken. With open enrollment approaching, increasing costs and decreasing benefits are in the news. But a less discussed issue is that the array of charges and benefits is now so complex that a reasonable consumer cannot make an informed decision. 
 In Kennebec County alone, the 32 Advantage plans that include drug coverage differ in at least 11 respects. Without even considering medications, an informed consumer would have to consider 352 data points in various combinations in order to choose her best plan. 
 Excluding the plans marketed exclusively to those with special needs, there are still 17 plans requiring the consideration of 187 data points. Dental coverage is particularly vexing, with its disorienting set of copayments, co-insurances, covered and uncovered services, in- and out-of-network coverage and premiums. The result is a mind-boggling array of choices that stultify rather than clarify consumer choices. 
 In 1990, the federal government simplified the Medigap marketplace by requiring insurers to offer set menus of benefits from which beneficiaries can choose. Insurance companies then compete based on price and service. Applying this framework to the muddle that is Medicare Advantage would turn it into a workable system that allows consumers to make informed decisions.
 Eileen Ringel 
 Oakland
